title: White Fish vs Oily Fish: Nutrition Differences and Examples

seo.title: White vs Oily Fish: Protein, Fat and Omega-3
seo.meta_description: Lean white fish is lower in fat and calories; oily fish provides far more EPA and DHA. Protein is often similar across both groups.
seo.search_intent: Explain the real nutritional differences between lean white fish and oily fish using examples, protein, fat, calories and omega-3.

excerpt: Lean white fish often provides roughly 80–130 calories per 100 grams cooked, while oily fish can reach 180–250 because it contains more fat. That extra fat also carries far more EPA and DHA. Protein is often similar across both groups at roughly 18–25 grams per 100 grams.
content_html:
‘White fish’ and ‘oily fish’ do not separate fish with protein from fish without it, or good fish from bad fish. The main nutritional difference is the amount of fat stored in the flesh.

Lean fish is usually lower in calories; oily fish carries more energy because it contains more fat, but it also supplies much more EPA and DHA. Protein can be remarkably similar.

Examples that make the categories easier to understand

Common lean or white fish include cod, haddock, pollock, sole and many types of hake. Oily or fatty fish include salmon, sardines, Atlantic mackerel and herring.

The boundary is not perfectly fixed. Fat content changes with species, season, feeding and life stage. The categories are useful nutritional shorthand rather than an exact chemical threshold.

A representative cooked comparison

Per 100 g cookedLean white fishOily fish
Calories~80–130~180–250
Protein~18–24 g~20–25 g
Fat~1–3 g~8–15 g
EPA + DHAOften ~0.1–0.4 gOften ~1–2+ g

Protein overlaps heavily. Most of the calorie difference comes from fat: fat supplies about 9 calories per gram versus about 4 per gram for protein.

Cod and haddock deliver protein with very little fat

A cooked lean fish can provide around 20–23 grams of protein per 100 grams while containing only a small amount of fat. That makes it efficient when the goal is a high-protein meal with relatively few calories.

Cooking method can change the final dish dramatically. Breaded fried cod no longer has the same calorie and fat profile as baked, steamed or broiled cod.

Salmon, sardines and mackerel bring more energy and far more omega-3

Cooked Atlantic salmon contains roughly 12 grams of fat per 100 grams and can provide around 2 grams of EPA+DHA. Sardines and Atlantic mackerel also sit far above very lean fish for long-chain omega-3.

Calling oily fish simply ‘higher fat’ therefore leaves out why much of that fat is nutritionally interesting.

Vitamin D often favors several fatty fish too

Salmon, sardines, herring and mackerel can provide meaningful vitamin D, although amounts vary widely by species and product. Lean fish still provide micronutrients, but many species contain less fat and fewer fat-soluble vitamins.

Mercury is not a lean-versus-fatty issue

Mercury depends mainly on species, size, lifespan and place in the food chain. Salmon and sardines are fatty fish and appear in FDA/EPA's Best Choices category.

So it is not accurate to assume fatty fish means more mercury or white fish means less. The species matters.

You do not have to choose one group

Using both makes nutritional sense: lean fish supplies very efficient protein, while oily fish adds much larger amounts of EPA and DHA and often vitamin D.

The useful rule

White fish is not better because it is lower in fat, and oily fish is not worse because it has more calories. They solve different nutritional jobs: one delivers lean protein; the other delivers protein plus marine fats that lean fish usually contains in much smaller amounts.

faq.question: What is the difference between white fish and oily fish?
faq.answer: The main difference is fat content. Lean white fish often contains around 1–3 g/100 g, while many oily fish contain roughly 8–15 g/100 g.

faq.question: Which has more protein?
faq.answer: Neither group has a clear advantage; both commonly provide around 18–25 grams per 100 grams cooked.

faq.question: Which has more omega-3?
faq.answer: Oily fish generally provides much more EPA and DHA, especially salmon, sardines, Atlantic mackerel and herring.
